summary: This standards-track RFC extends OSPF so that nodes can be given administrative tags, grouping them for policy purposes. Operators can then use the tags to simplify management and to control route and path selection through configured policies.

eli5.summary: You can stick colored labels on routers, like all the red ones, and then make rules that apply to every router with a given label.

questions: how to tag ospf nodes for policy
what is an ospf node admin tag
how are ospf node tags used in policy
what is the ospf router information lsa
subtitle: Letting OSPF routers carry opaque 32-bit labels so operators can group nodes and write policies about them.

tldr.problem: Operators want to group routers by role or location and apply policies to the whole group, but OSPF had no standard way to advertise such a label for a node.
tldr.mechanism: A new Node Admin Tag TLV (type 10) in the OSPF Router Information LSA carries one or more 32-bit administrative tags, whose meaning is defined only by local policy.
tldr.outcome: Tags let policies such as LFA selection, tunnel tail-end choice and path pruning be written once per group instead of once per router. The tags have no meaning to OSPF itself.

today: RFC 7777 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the RI LSA of RFC 7770.

sections.title: Tagging Nodes in OSPF
sections.content:
RFC 7777 adds an optional capability to OSPF: giving a router a node administrative tag and using it as an attribute of that node. The RFC gives two example uses: Traffic Engineering applications that want different path-selection criteria, and preferring or pruning paths when selecting Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) backups through local policy.

Route and path selection applies to both TE and non-TE uses, so the tags are carried in a new TLV inside the Router Information (RI) Link State Advertisement defined in RFC 7770. Tags may be used by OSPF itself or by other applications that consume information propagated via OSPF. The document covers both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
sections.eli5: Imagine putting a sticker on each router saying what job it does. Then you can write a rule like 'only use routers with the blue sticker'.

sections.title: The Node Admin Tag TLV
sections.content:
An administrative tag is a 32-bit integer that identifies a group of nodes in the OSPF domain. The Node Admin Tag TLV has Type 10, a 16-bit Length field that counts the value in octets (always a multiple of 4), and a Value made of one or more 32-bit tags. At least one tag MUST be carried if the TLV is included.

The TLV travels in an RI LSA for both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. An RI LSA can have link, area or Autonomous System flooding scope, and which scope to use for tags is a matter of local policy. A node advertises the set of groups it belongs to, for example all PE nodes with one tag value and all P nodes with another. Multiple Node Admin Tag TLVs MAY appear in the same RI LSA or in different instances of it.
sections.eli5: The sticker is just a long number. A router can wear several stickers, and it announces them all in one message to its neighbors.

sections.title: How Tags Are Interpreted and Processed
sections.content:
The meaning of a tag is generally opaque to OSPF. It is defined by the network's local policy and set by configuration, so tag values SHOULD NOT be propagated outside the administrative domain they apply to. A router that does not understand a tag or has no matching policy ignores that tag and floods the RI LSA unchanged.

The order of tags has no meaning, and the list MUST be treated as unordered. Each tag is an independent identifier, and policies may test for several tags together (tag A AND tag B) but MUST NOT depend on order.

Tags are not meant to be extended by future OSPF standards and do not require IANA registration. Because they live in the RI LSA, they must be reasonably small and stable, and they MUST NOT be used to convey routing topology attributes or to track topology or reachability changes.

For processing, the tags a node originates SHOULD be treated as the superset of all tags from all its RI LSA instances in the Link-State Database. When the set of tags changes, a node MUST re-originate its RI LSA, and receivers that have features depending on the tags MUST repeat the relevant computation.
sections.eli5: OSPF just passes the stickers along without knowing what they mean. Each network decides its own meanings, and the order of the stickers does not matter.

sections.title: Example Applications
sections.content:
The RFC lists examples only to show how generally useful tagging is; implementations are not required to support any of them.

  • Service auto-discovery: tag every PE router and configure a policy to build MPLS TE tunnels to all routers with that tag. When a new PE router joins, the others open tunnels to it without reconfiguration.
  • Fast-reroute policy: give each layer (Access, Distribution, Core) a tag, so that a Distribution device computes LFA only via Distribution or Core neighbors. Excluding neighbors known to provide no valid LFA can also cut the number of Dijkstra runs.
  • Remote LFA tunnel termination: accept only routers with a certain tag as tail-end candidates, which excludes unsuitable nodes or defines a region for the choice.
  • Mobile backhaul: assign tags to nodes in different rings so TE path computation can respect extra constraints.
  • Explicit routing policy: tag A, I, R and T nodes by role. To forbid traffic from A nodes to I nodes passing through R and T nodes, run a CSPF on A nodes that excludes nodes tagged I for destinations tagged A.
sections.eli5: Stickers let you say 'build roads to every house with a red sticker', 'never route through the school zone', or 'only pick helpers from this neighborhood', without listing each house.

sections.title: Operations and Manageability
sections.content:
Operators assign tag meanings that are local to their administrative domain. The RFC compares operational use to IS-IS prefix tags and BGP communities, and says the discipline used for those applies here too. Defining a policy language is out of scope.

A caution: pruning policies can remove a path from the forwarding plane entirely, so they have more severe potential impact, such as node unreachability, than preference policies that only influence path selection.

For manageability, tags are configured through routing policy enhancements. The OSPF YANG data model and the routing policy model are expected to be enhanced to cover node administrative tags.
sections.eli5: Stickers that only say 'prefer this' are mild. Stickers that say 'never use this road' can cut a town off if you get them wrong, so be careful.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Tags may be used to indicate geographical location or other sensitive information. OSPF authentication does not provide confidentiality, so tag contents could leak to an IGP snooper. Confidentiality can be obtained by running OSPF over IPsec tunnels or using the IPsec-based mechanisms of RFC 4552. Advertising tags from one administrative domain into another risks misinterpretation if the domains assign different meanings to the same values.

The generic routing and OSPF threats in RFC 4593 and RFC 6863 also apply. OSPF authentication or the extended mechanisms of RFC 7474 or RFC 7166 SHOULD be used where attackers can reach the physical network. IANA registered Node Admin Tag TLV value 10 in the "OSPF Router Information (RI) TLVs" registry.
sections.eli5: A sticker might reveal something private, like where a router sits. Keep the stickers inside your own network and lock the messages if you need to.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value in octets, a multiple of 4.

fields.name: Administrative Tag #1
fields.desc: First 32-bit tag; at least one tag is required.

fields.name: Administrative Tag #N
fields.desc: Further tags, in no meaningful order.
